title: Fluoride: how it works & how it's delivered
blurb: How fluoride protects teeth, the Delivering Better Oral Health toothpaste rules by age, and every way fluoride reaches the mouth.
question: A mother says she puts a full strip of her own toothpaste on her 4-year-old's brush, then rinses his mouth out with water 'to get the toothpaste out'. What would you advise about the amount, the strength and the rinsing, and why?

teach.h: The most effective caries protection there is
teach.body: Fluoride is a naturally occurring mineral that makes teeth more resistant to decay. Brushing twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste is the single most effective thing a patient can do at home to prevent caries. It benefits every age group, not just children: adults with exposed roots, dry mouth or new decay gain just as much. Your job is to make sure patients use the right strength, the right amount, at the right times.

children.label: Fluorapatite
children.sub: Enamel crystal more resistant to acid

teach.caption: Fluoride replaces part of the hydroxyapatite crystal, forming fluorapatite, which dissolves at a lower pH.

teach.h: Little and often, at the tooth surface
teach.body: Fluoride works mainly topically, after the teeth have erupted. Low levels kept in saliva and plaque all day slow down mineral loss when plaque acid drops the pH, and speed up mineral gain when the pH recovers. That is why regular, small doses work best: brushing twice a day, spitting out rather than rinsing, and using a mouthrinse at a different time from brushing. Rinsing with water straight after brushing washes this protective fluoride away.

teach.h: What fluoride can and can't fix
teach.caption: First and third teeth: an early white spot lesion in the enamel (cut-through and outside views), which fluoride and good brushing can help remineralise. Second and fourth: decay has broken through into dentine and needs the dentist to restore it.

head: Who
Fluoride strength
Key point
teach.caption: All: brush at least twice a day, last thing at night and one other time. A smear gives about 0.1 mg fluoride; a pea-sized amount about 0.25 mg.
Prescription pastes and varnish are for patients with active caries or higher risk, prescribed or applied by the dental team.

teach.h: Getting the most from fluoride toothpaste
items: Use fluoride toothpaste every time you brush, at least twice a day.
Make one session last thing at night, when saliva flow drops during sleep.
Use the right amount for age: a smear under 3, pea-sized from 3.
Spit out the excess after brushing. Don't rinse with water or mouthwash.
If a fluoride mouthrinse is advised, use it at a different time, for example after lunch.

teach.body: Fluoride mouthrinse (0.05% sodium fluoride, 230 ppm) is used daily at a different time from brushing by patients giving concern (children from 7, and adults), and may be recommended for anyone aged 8 or over with active caries. Fluoride varnish (22,600 ppm) is painted on by the dental team two or more times a year. The dentist may prescribe 2,800 ppm toothpaste from age 10, or 2,800 or 5,000 ppm from age 16, for active caries. At population level, water fluoridation adjusts fluoride in drinking water to around 1 ppm.

teach.h: Why amounts matter for children: fluorosis
teach.body: If a young child regularly swallows too much fluoride while their teeth are still forming, the enamel can develop fluorosis: usually faint white flecks or lines, and in more severe cases brown mottling. This is why young children use only a smear or a pea-sized amount, why parents should brush or supervise, and why children should spit out and not eat toothpaste. Used as DBOH advises, the caries benefit far outweighs this risk.

teach.text: Rinsing with water, or using a mouthwash straight after brushing, washes the fluoride off the teeth. The advice is 'spit, don't rinse', and any fluoride mouthrinse goes at a different time of day.

items: Fluoride forms acid-resistant fluorapatite, boosts remineralisation and reduces bacterial acid.
Under 3: smear of at least 1,000 ppm. 3–6: pea-sized, at least 1,000 ppm. 7+ and adults: 1,350–1,500 ppm.
Brush twice daily (one session last thing at night), spit, don't rinse.
Mouthrinse 230 ppm at a different time; varnish 22,600 ppm; prescription 2,800 (10+) or 5,000 ppm (16+).
Fluoride benefits all ages; too much swallowed by young children risks fluorosis.

summary: You can now explain the three ways fluoride protects teeth, give DBOH toothpaste advice by age (strength and amount), explain 'spit, don't rinse' and when to use a mouthrinse, compare the strengths of toothpaste, rinse, prescription paste and varnish, and explain why young children's fluoride intake is controlled.

A.q: A parent asks how much toothpaste to use for their 2-year-old. What does DBOH advise?
options: A smear of at least 1,000 ppm
A full strip of children's paste
A.why: For children up to 3, DBOH advises a smear of toothpaste containing at least 1,000 ppm fluoride, brushed by a parent.

whyNot.0: A pea-sized amount is the advice from age 3, not for a 2-year-old.
whyNot.2: A full strip is far too much for a young child and increases fluorosis risk.
whyNot.3: Brushing with fluoride toothpaste should start as soon as the first tooth erupts.

A.q: A patient rinses vigorously with water after brushing. What is the best advice?
options: Spit out the excess, don't rinse
Rinse until the minty taste has gone
A.why: Spitting out without rinsing leaves fluoride on the teeth and in saliva, where it keeps protecting the enamel.

whyNot.0: Rinsing with any water still washes the fluoride away.
whyNot.1: Using mouthwash straight after brushing also rinses away the more concentrated toothpaste fluoride.
whyNot.3: Rinsing until the taste goes removes the fluoride you want to stay on the teeth.

A.q: How does fluoride make enamel more resistant to acid attack?
A.why: Fluoride is taken into the enamel crystal to form fluorapatite, which dissolves at a lower pH than hydroxyapatite.

whyNot.0: Sealing tubules relates to desensitising agents, not fluoride's anti-caries action.
whyNot.1: Fluoride doesn't add thickness; enamel can't regrow.
whyNot.2: Fluoride doesn't neutralise acid in drinks; saliva's buffers do that in the mouth.

B.q: A patient uses a fluoride mouthrinse straight after brushing. What should you advise?
options: Use it at a different time of day
Swallow a small amount of it
Stop the toothpaste and keep the rinse
B.why: Using the rinse at a separate time, such as after lunch, adds an extra fluoride contact instead of washing away the toothpaste.

whyNot.1: Rinsing just before brushing doesn't add a separate fluoride contact.
whyNot.2: Fluoride mouthrinse should be spat out, not swallowed.
whyNot.3: Toothpaste is the main fluoride source; the rinse is an addition, not a replacement.

B.q: What fluoride concentration does DBOH recommend in toothpaste for a healthy 9-year-old?
B.why: From 7 years old, DBOH recommends a toothpaste containing 1,350–1,500 ppm fluoride.

whyNot.0: At least 1,000 ppm is the minimum for children under 7.
whyNot.2: 2,800 ppm is a prescription paste considered from age 10 for active caries.
whyNot.3: 5,000 ppm is a prescription paste considered from age 16 for active caries.

B.q: A patient says fluoride is only useful for children. How should you respond?
options: Agree, as adult enamel is fully formed
Agree, unless the patient has dentures
Explain that adults benefit only from varnish
Explain fluoride protects teeth at all ages
B.why: Fluoride works mainly topically on erupted teeth, so it protects adults' teeth, including exposed roots, throughout life.

whyNot.0: Fluoride's main effect is topical after eruption, so adults benefit fully.
whyNot.1: Dentures don't need fluoride, but any natural teeth do.
whyNot.2: Adults benefit from twice-daily fluoride toothpaste, not just professional varnish.

C.q: A patient brushes once a day with fluoride toothpaste but keeps developing new decay. What is the best first advice?
options: Brush harder at that one session
Use a non-fluoride paste for a week
C.why: DBOH advises brushing with fluoride toothpaste at least twice daily, including last thing at night.

whyNot.0: Brushing harder risks abrasion and doesn't add fluoride contact.
whyNot.1: Rinsing would remove fluoride, making things worse.
whyNot.3: Removing fluoride would increase caries risk.

C.q: Which statement about fluoride varnish is correct?
options: It is used daily at home
It is only for adults with active caries
C.why: Fluoride varnish is 2.26% sodium fluoride, which is 22,600 ppm fluoride, applied by the dental team.

whyNot.0: 1,450 ppm is a typical family toothpaste strength.
whyNot.1: Varnish is applied professionally, typically twice or more a year, not daily at home.
whyNot.3: DBOH recommends varnish for all children from 3 years, as well as adults giving concern.

C.q: Why should young children use only a smear or a pea-sized amount of toothpaste?
options: To reduce the risk of fluorosis
To stop the paste irritating gums
C.why: Swallowing too much fluoride while teeth are forming can cause fluorosis, so the amount is controlled by age.

whyNot.1: Fluoride doesn't stain baby teeth at toothpaste levels.
whyNot.2: Fluoride prevents decay; the limit is about fluorosis, not caries.
whyNot.3: Gum irritation isn't the reason for age-based amounts.

reteach.title: Fluoride as a repair crew
reteach.question: Imagine your enamel is a brick wall that acid chips away at every time you eat sugar. How does fluoride help keep the wall standing?

blocks.body: Every sugary snack sends an acid attack that knocks bits out of the wall. Saliva is a repair crew that puts minerals back afterwards. Fluoride makes that crew faster, and the replacement bricks it lays (fluorapatite) are tougher than the originals. It also slows the attackers by reducing how much acid the bacteria make. But the crew can only work if fluoride is there, which is why you leave it on the teeth (spit, don't rinse) and top it up twice a day.

blocks.text: Children's amount: SMEAR under 3, PEA-SIZED from 3. Strength: at least 1,000 ppm under 7; 1,350–1,500 ppm from 7 (or younger if giving concern).

explain.body: Fluoride forms acid-resistant fluorapatite, helps remineralise early lesions and reduces bacterial acid production. It works mainly topically, so small regular doses at the tooth surface are what count.

test.q: Which of these is NOT a way fluoride helps prevent caries?
test.why: Fluoride reduces bacterial acid production but doesn't kill all plaque bacteria; plaque still needs removing by brushing.

whyNot.0: Promoting remineralisation is a key action of fluoride.
whyNot.1: Forming fluorapatite makes enamel more acid-resistant.
whyNot.2: Fluoride interferes with bacterial enzymes, reducing acid production.

explain.body: Under 3: smear, at least 1,000 ppm. 3–6: pea-sized, at least 1,000 ppm. From 7: 1,350–1,500 ppm. Children giving concern under 7 also use 1,350–1,500 ppm.

test.q: A 5-year-old has had several fillings and is giving concern. What toothpaste strength does DBOH advise?
test.why: For children aged 0–6 giving concern, DBOH advises toothpaste containing 1,350–1,500 ppm fluoride.

whyNot.0: At least 1,000 ppm is the advice for children under 7 who are not giving concern.
whyNot.2: 2,800 ppm is only considered from age 10.
whyNot.3: Fluoride-free paste gives no caries protection.

explain.body: After brushing, spit out the excess and don't rinse with water or mouthwash. That keeps fluoride on the teeth. A fluoride mouthrinse, if advised, is used at a different time of day.

rows.label: Brush, spit out, leave the rest

test.q: Which routine gives the best fluoride benefit?
test.why: Spitting without rinsing keeps toothpaste fluoride on the teeth, and a mouthrinse at a separate time adds another fluoride contact.

whyNot.0: Rinsing and using mouthwash straight after brushing washes the toothpaste fluoride away.
whyNot.2: Rinsing after brushing removes the fluoride.
whyNot.3: Swallowing foam isn't advised, and rinsing removes fluoride.

explain.body: Mouthrinse 230 ppm daily (children 7+ and adults giving concern; considered for anyone 8+ with active caries). Varnish 22,600 ppm by the dental team. Prescription toothpaste 2,800 ppm from age 10; 2,800 or 5,000 ppm from age 16.

test.q: A 12-year-old has active caries. Which prescription toothpaste might the dentist consider?
test.why: DBOH says 2,800 ppm toothpaste can be considered from age 10 for active caries; 5,000 ppm is for 16 and over.

whyNot.1: 5,000 ppm paste is only considered from age 16.
whyNot.2: 22,600 ppm is the strength of varnish, not toothpaste.
whyNot.3: 230 ppm is the strength of a daily mouthrinse.
